statement: Jo has one minute left and 3 blank questions. She knows one answer, has a hunch about another, and no idea about the third. Wrong answers cost nothing. What should she do?

choices.text: answer none of them, as there is no time
choices.misconception: I thought a minute was too short, but marking a choice takes only a few seconds.

choices.text: answer only the one she knows
choices.misconception: I thought guessing was risky, but a wrong answer costs nothing.

choices.text: answer the two she has some idea about
choices.misconception: I left the third one blank, but a blank scores zero for sure and a guess might score.

choices.text: it depends on how many points each one is worth
choices.misconception: I thought guessing a big question was riskier, but nothing is taken off for any wrong answer.

hints: Compare a blank with a guess. A blank always scores nothing. A guess might be right and costs nothing if it is wrong. So a guess is never worse than a blank.
Mark the answer she knows, mark her hunch, and mark any choice for the last one. All three take only seconds.

solutions.reliable: A blank always scores zero. A marked answer scores if it is right and loses nothing if it is wrong, so marking is never worse than leaving a blank. Jo should mark the one she knows, mark her hunch, and pick any choice for the third. The idea to keep: when wrong answers cost nothing, never leave a question blank.

whyOnTest: Knowing that a blank can only score zero is a free gain on every Kangaroo paper.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
